body:
The Indian summer monsoon and tropical circulation

The Indian monsoon illustrates how seasonal migration of pressure systems can substantially modify the general planetary wind circulation.

During Northern Hemisphere summer, the Indian subcontinent becomes intensely heated. A region of low atmospheric pressure develops over northern and northwestern India, while relatively high pressure persists over parts of the southern Indian Ocean.

The resulting pressure distribution, together with the northward displacement of tropical convergence, encourages the movement of air from the Southern Hemisphere towards the Indian subcontinent.

The ITCZ and the monsoon trough

During July, the tropical convergence zone over the Indian region may extend to approximately 20° N to 25° N, over the Gangetic Plain.

This northward-displaced low-pressure and convergence zone is associated with the monsoon trough, an elongated region of relatively low atmospheric pressure over the Indian subcontinent.

The monsoon trough favours the convergence and ascent of moisture-bearing winds and plays an important role in organising summer monsoon rainfall.

Its precise location varies with atmospheric conditions. The 20° N to 25° N range is a useful textbook approximation for the July circulation pattern rather than a fixed boundary.

How southeast trade winds become southwest monsoon winds

The formation of the southwest monsoon can be understood through the combined effects of seasonal pressure differences and Earth's rotation.

  1. Southeast trade winds originate from the subtropical high-pressure region over the southern Indian Ocean.
  2. The northward displacement of tropical low pressure draws part of this airflow towards the Indian subcontinent.
  3. In the conventional textbook description, these winds cross the Equator over the western Indian Ocean, approximately between 40° E and 60° E longitudes.
  4. After entering the Northern Hemisphere, the airflow is deflected towards its right by the Coriolis effect.
  5. The winds acquire a predominantly southwesterly direction and transport moisture from the Indian Ocean towards India.

Thus, the southwest monsoon can be understood partly as the continuation of Southern Hemisphere southeast trade winds after they cross the Equator and change direction.

Crossing the Equator

Southeast trade winds originate in the Southern Hemisphere. After crossing into the Northern Hemisphere, their direction changes under rightward Coriolis deflection. They approach India predominantly as southwest monsoon winds, not as southeast trade winds.

Winter reversal of winds

During Northern Hemisphere winter, the Indian landmass cools and relatively high pressure develops over the continent. The tropical convergence zone retreats southward.

These changes favour a reversal of the prevailing circulation. Northeasterly winds generally move from the Asian landmass towards the surrounding seas.

Because they originate mainly over land, these winds are comparatively dry over much of India. However, some winds acquire moisture while crossing the Bay of Bengal and contribute to rainfall along the southeastern coast, particularly the Tamil Nadu coast.

Seasonal movement of the ITCZ and differences in land and ocean heating explain important aspects of this reversal. The complete monsoon mechanism also involves other large-scale atmospheric processes.

Connection with Gujarat

Gujarat lies along the western side of the Indian subcontinent, adjoining the Arabian Sea. The Arabian Sea branch of the southwest monsoon is an important source of moisture for the state.

During the summer monsoon, moisture-bearing winds move towards western India. Part of this airflow reaches Gujarat, Saurashtra and Kachchh and continues towards Rajasthan.

The summer monsoon is especially important for rainfed agriculture in Gujarat. In southern Gujarat, the arrival of moisture-bearing monsoon winds supports agricultural activities such as the cultivation of rice during the rainy season.

Nevertheless, proximity to the Arabian Sea does not guarantee uniform rainfall across Gujarat. Regional relief, atmospheric disturbances and the changing position of monsoon circulation contribute to differences in rainfall between southern Gujarat and the drier northwestern parts of the state.

Distinguishing planetary winds from monsoon winds

FeaturePlanetary windsMonsoon winds
ClassificationPermanent or prevailingSeasonal or periodic
DirectionBroadly persistent within wind beltsMarked seasonal change or reversal
Principal controlsGlobal pressure belts and Earth's rotationSeasonal pressure redistribution and regional circulation
ExampleSoutheast trade windsSouthwest monsoon over India

The two categories are related rather than completely independent. Seasonal redistribution of pressure can redirect a planetary wind into a regional monsoon circulation.

Integrated revision of global pressure and wind circulation

Unequal solar heating contributes to planetary pressure differences. The pressure gradient force initiates air movement, while Earth's rotation deflects horizontal winds to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere. The resulting prevailing surface wind systems connect the major pressure belts.

Trade winds flow from subtropical highs near 30° towards the equatorial low, westerlies connect subtropical highs near 30° with subpolar lows near 60°, and polar easterlies connect polar highs near 90° with subpolar lows.

Trade-wind convergence helps maintain the ITCZ, whose seasonal migration modifies the global wind pattern. Its pronounced northward displacement over South Asia during summer contributes to cross-equatorial airflow and the Indian southwest monsoon.

Prelims focus

  • July ITCZ position over the Indian region: approximately 20° N–25° N.
  • Textbook cross-equatorial monsoon airflow: approximately 40° E–60° E.
  • Southern Hemisphere southeast trades contribute to India's southwest monsoon.
  • Coriolis deflection becomes rightward after the airflow enters the Northern Hemisphere.
  • The Arabian Sea branch supplies important monsoon moisture to Gujarat.
  • Trap: The ITCZ is not the sole cause of the entire Indian monsoon mechanism.

[References: NCERT, India: Physical Environment, Class 11, 2025–26 reprint, Chapter 4: Climate, p. 30, Inter Tropical Convergence Zone and Onset of the Monsoon; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Social Science, Standard 9, Chapter 16: Climate, pp. 125–127; NCERT, Contemporary India–I, Class 9, Chapter 4: Climate, Advancing Monsoon and Cold Weather Season; NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, 2025–26 reprint, Chapter 9, pp. 77–80. Online sources consulted on 28 November 2026.]
